analysis.one_liner: Spends billions on affordable internet for low-income households and opens the market to city-owned broadband.
analysis.headline: Backed by 19 senators, all Democrats, the bill sat in the Senate Commerce Committee for the entire two-year Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would spend billions of dollars to make internet service affordable and available: bigger subsidies for low-income households' internet bills, grants for devices and digital skills training, low-interest loans for building networks, and rules requiring providers to disclose their prices to consumers. It would also override state laws that keep cities, co-ops, and public-private partnerships from offering their own broadband, opening the market to public competition. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households earning up to 150% of the poverty line, along with seniors, veterans, people with disabilities, rural and tribal residents, and others the bill defines as "covered populations," would gain cheaper internet, subsidized devices, and digital literacy training. Rural health clinics, schools, and school buses would gain funding for connectivity. Cities, rural electric co-ops, and nonprofits that want to build or offer broadband would gain access to low-cost financing and would no longer be barred by state laws from serving customers.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes an additional $6 billion for the Emergency Broadband Connectivity Fund, which subsidizes internet service for low-income households, and authorizes $200 million to connect state benefits databases so eligibility for the Lifeline and emergency broadband programs can be verified automatically.

Creates digital equity grant programs — $625 million for state capacity grants and $625 million for competitive grants — to fund devices, public computing centers, and digital literacy training for low-income households, seniors, veterans, people with disabilities, and other covered populations.
Requires the FCC to collect broadband pricing data and adopt standardized consumer labels disclosing information about broadband plans.
Preempts state laws that prohibit cities, public providers, and public-private partnerships from offering high-speed broadband, opening those markets to public competition.

Makes low-interest loans and lines of credit available for broadband infrastructure, requires broadband conduit to be installed during certain highway projects, and funds school-bus Wi-Fi, rural health care connectivity, and internet exchange facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through appropriations across fiscal years 2022 through 2026 for the subsidy, grant, loan, and study programs. Incumbent cable and telephone companies would also bear costs: they would face new public competitors in states that currently shield them, and mandatory price disclosure would expose their pricing to comparison. The bill's grant programs also attach labor conditions, including prevailing wages for construction work.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes billions of dollars in new federal spending from 2022 through 2026 across its subsidy, grant, and infrastructure programs, all paid for through appropriations.

The bill itself acknowledges a risk that subsidies could backfire: it requires a federal study of how to deliver subsidies 'to ensure that the availability of the subsidies does not result in providers raising the price of broadband service for households receiving subsidies.'

Preempting state laws on community broadband takes away decisions state legislatures made about whether public providers may compete in their own markets, a significant assertion of federal power over state telecommunications policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households that cannot afford internet, the benefits are direct and large: subsidized service, free or cheap devices, and training, alongside visible pricing and the chance of a cheaper public option. The main honest costs are the multi-billion-dollar federal price tag and the real risk the bill itself flags — that subsidies passed through providers could push retail prices up rather than down. The community-broadband preemption is a genuine federalism tradeoff, but its effect is to remove legal barriers that keep a potentially cheaper competitor out of the market.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar and 13 original cosponsors introduced the bill in the Senate on March 15, 2021.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Eighteen additional senators, all Democrats, had signed on as cosponsors by the end of the Congress.
The action history shows no further activity of any kind — no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote — through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband providers came out ahead: the bill's price-transparency rules and its preemption of state laws blocking city-owned broadband died with it. Low-income households lost a chance at expanded subsidies, though Congress funded broadband separately in other legislation later that year, so the loss was partly offset elsewhere.

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led 13 original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the two-year action history.

against.name: Cable and telecom industry lobbying groups
against.role: Incumbent broadband providers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed municipal-broadband preemption and price-regulation proposals during this period, backing state laws the bill would have overridden.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 senators behind the bill — the sponsor plus 18 cosponsors — were Democrats (18 of the Senate's 48); no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote that would have produced a roll-call breakdown.

industries.industry: Cable and telephone broadband providers (incumbent ISPs)
industries.note: The bill would expose their pricing through mandatory consumer labels and would open their markets to city-owned and cooperative competitors by preempting state bans — the provisions most directly against their interest. At the same time, its household subsidies would flow to these same providers as the entities paid for low-income customers' service, reinforcing their role as the channel for federal internet aid.

industries.industry: Municipal utilities, rural co-ops, and public broadband providers
industries.note: The bill would invalidate state laws that prohibit these public and partnership providers from offering high-speed broadband, letting them compete where they currently cannot.

industries.industry: Telecom construction and network equipment contractors
industries.note: Bill-financed infrastructure — loans, grants, dig-once conduit requirements, and community networks — would generate construction and equipment work, with grant-funded construction required to pay prevailing wages.
They would be eligible grantees for digital equity funding to supply devices, training, and public computing access to covered populations.
